premortem_risks: Next.js major-version upgrade (14→15/16) introduces breaking changes across 40+ routes that typecheck/lint/unit-tests don't catch (caching semantics, middleware behavior, App Router changes) — could silently break something the existing test suite doesn't cover.

Obscura sidecar integration requires Docker/CI infrastructure changes (new Dockerfile stage, compose service, GitHub Actions service container) — a category with less local test coverage than pure application code; CI-only networking failures may not surface until push.

The two tracks (Next.js upgrade, Obscura build) both touch shared config files (package.json, docker-compose.yml, CI workflow yaml) — sequential work on one risks lockfile/dependency conflicts with the other, the same class of collision already hit earlier this session between concurrent workstreams.
The 3-day deadline is tight — Next.js major-version migrations commonly run multi-day in real projects; real risk of the deadline slipping if m1's audit reveals more breakage than expected.
premortem_mitigations: After the Next.js bump, do a full live browser click-through of the actual running app (not just a clean `next build`) covering the core flows already verified this session, before marking m3 done.

Verify the Obscura service container starts and responds in a LOCAL docker-compose run before ever pushing a CI workflow change; treat the CI service-container step as its own explicit milestone (m9) with a dry-run push to confirm before folding into the main branch.

Fully commit+push each track's package.json/lockfile changes before starting the other track's dependency changes; re-run `npm ci` (not just `npm install`) after each track to catch lockfile desync immediately — the exact fix already applied earlier today.

If m1's compatibility audit shows the migration is bigger than a 1-day task, flag it to Tony immediately and propose descoping to Next.js 15 (smaller jump) instead of 16, or extending the deadline — rather than silently blowing past 2026-07-04.
